issues.title: support prague / l4s congestion response
issues.author: kazuho
issues.body:
ABBA currently assumes that each congestion event reduces the congestion window by a fixed multiplicative factor beta. The same machinery can be applied to Prague/L4S with relatively little change.

When queue buildup is not visible, ABBA accelerates the increase once:

```c
cwnd > cwnd_prior * (2 - beta)
```

Prague reduces the congestion window on CE feedback using approximately:

```c
beta = 1 - alpha / 2
```

where alpha is Prague's EWMA estimate of the CE-marked fraction.

By simply recording the effective beta used for each congestion-window reduction, ABBA can use that recorded value for the following congestion epoch. The existing ABBA rules, including the acceleration threshold above, can then be applied unchanged.

Prague uses a CUBIC arm on a per-period basis, as in Apple's implementation. That arm can use the existing ABBA behavior unchanged.

Prague's existing adaptation of alpha can also remain unchanged. If ABBA accelerates too aggressively and causes a higher CE-marking fraction, Prague will naturally increase alpha, resulting in a stronger subsequent reduction. Therefore, no ABBA-specific adjustment of alpha appears necessary.

pulls.title: fix the window of the low point at recovery exit; let only its RTT fall
pulls.author: kazuho
pulls.body:
## Problem

The low point used to move, as a whole, to any sample carrying a round-trip
time at least 1ms below low_rtt: low_cwnd jumped to the window then in hand.
Refitting through that point makes the model predict exactly the observed RTT
at the current window, so the gain collapses to zero at the moment the path
shows room. Under jitter the minimum filter keeps finding new lows, each one
re-anchoring low_cwnd and resetting the growth that had built up; a gradually
shallower base RTT has the same effect. The 1ms threshold was meant to keep
jitter from doing this, but the cause was low_cwnd moving, not the size of the
step.

This is the reported failure on 5G paths switching to carrier aggregation:
capacity jumps, yet ABBA ramps up slowly once the path has some jitter.

## Change

* low_cwnd stays at the window on leaving recovery, the smallest of the period
  and hence where the queue is shortest.
* low_rtt takes any lower sample, with no threshold. Under the model, later
  samples are taken at larger windows, so they fall below the RTT recorded at
  low_cwnd only where that observation was inflated by jitter; the lowest of
  them is the better estimate of the RTT at low_cwnd.
* low_rtt is no longer updated once the model has been redrawn from the origin
  (Beyond the Observed Range). Refitting through the low point there would
  revive the abandoned line far outside its range, letting a lower RTT lower
  the prediction being pursued.
* fit() loses the `high_cwnd <= low_cwnd` guard and the paragraph explaining
  it: low_cwnd now always lies below high_cwnd.
* The introduction and the model overview describe the low point accordingly.

## Evaluation

Implemented in quicly (lib/cc-pico.c; not yet committed there) and compared
against quicly master ("old") and stock CUBIC in the quicly simulator, which
was extended with a mid-run bandwidth/delay change (-S) and in-order jitter
applied after the bottleneck (-J).

Scenario: 5G profile (40ms base RTT, 80ms queue), one CUBIC flow with pacing,
bottleneck stepping from 100 to 500 Mbit/s. The switch time is swept over 20
points (40-59s) to cover the congestion epoch, crossed with jitter of
0/2/5ms and a base-delay shift of 0/-3ms at the switch; 120 runs per variant.

Time to reach 80% of 500 Mbit/s (seconds, p10/median/p90; 15 = not reached):

| jitter | delay shift | stock | old | new |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0ms | 0ms | 6.4/13.9/15.0 | 0.4/0.4/0.6 | 0.3/0.3/0.3 |
| 0ms | -3ms | 5.7/13.1/15.0 | 0.4/0.4/0.7 | 0.2/0.3/0.3 |
| 2ms | 0ms | 6.9/14.2/15.0 | 0.9/3.7/8.7 | 0.3/0.3/0.4 |
| 2ms | -3ms | 6.0/13.4/15.0 | 1.0/2.5/7.8 | 0.3/0.3/0.4 |
| 5ms | 0ms | 7.1/14.7/15.0 | 1.7/5.1/11.8 | 0.3/0.3/0.4 |
| 5ms | -3ms | 6.6/14.8/15.0 | 0.3/5.7/10.5 | 0.3/0.3/0.4 |

Mean goodput over the first 2s after the switch (Mbit/s):

| jitter | delay shift | stock | old | new |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0ms | 0ms | 262 | 446 | 475 |
| 0ms | -3ms | 284 | 457 | 478 |
| 2ms | 0ms | 253 | 304 | 470 |
| 2ms | -3ms | 272 | 315 | 459 |
| 5ms | 0ms | 242 | 266 | 469 |
| 5ms | -3ms | 256 | 291 | 464 |

By time since the last congestion event at the switch (all settings pooled;
time to 80%, p10/median/p90, with run counts):

| since congestion | stock | old | new |
|---|---|---|---|
| < 2s | 15.0/15.0/15.0 (25) | 0.4/1.2/10.8 (22) | 0.3/0.4/1.3 (21) |
| 2-5s | 13.9/15.0/15.0 (34) | 0.4/4.4/10.2 (36) | 0.3/0.3/0.4 (36) |
| >= 5s | 5.1/10.6/13.9 (61) | 0.3/1.7/7.1 (62) | 0.3/0.3/0.3 (63) |

Observations:

* Without jitter both ABBA variants are fast; with 2-5ms of jitter the old
  rule's median grows to 2.5-5.7s and its p90 to 8-12s, while the new rule
  stays at 0.3s (p90 <= 0.4s).
* Right after recovery the new rule has a slightly longer tail (p90 1.3s),
  still far below the old one (p90 10.8s).
* The first loss after the switch follows within 2s in 116/120 runs for the
  new rule (old: 62/120, stock: 0/120), as the faster ramp fills the 80ms
  queue sooner; mean goodput over the first 5s is unaffected (472-485 Mbit/s).

On a fixed-bandwidth LTE profile with random loss, and in two-flow fairness
runs, the differences between old and new were within run-to-run variation
at seven repetitions per cell; no flow was pushed below its fair share.

Limitations: one run per point, unpaired randomness, a single flow, uniform
jitter, and no capacity decrease.
